title: Two Sum
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice. Return the answer in any order.
examples:
Input: nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Output: [0, 1]

Input: nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6
Output: [1, 2]
constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 10^4
-10^9 <= nums[i], target <= 10^9
Exactly one valid answer exists.
solutionOutline: One pass with HashMap<Integer, Integer> from value to index. For each i, check whether target - nums[i] is already in the map; if so return [map.get(complement), i], otherwise store nums[i] -> i. O(n) time, O(n) space. Probe: why check before inserting (it handles nums = [3, 3], target 6 and never uses the same element twice). Brute force is O(n^2). Sorting with two pointers is O(n log n) but loses the original indices unless you keep pairs.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string s containing only the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine whether it is valid. Open brackets must be closed by the same type of bracket and in the correct order.
examples:
Input: s = "()[]{}"
Output: true

Input: s = "(]"
Output: false

Input: s = "([)]"
Output: false
solutionOutline: Use an ArrayDeque<Character> as a stack. Push openers. On a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. At the end the stack must be empty. O(n) time and space. Edge cases: a closer arriving with an empty stack, leftover openers, odd length (an early exit). Prefer ArrayDeque over Stack.

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.
solutionOutline: Sort by start with Arrays.sort(intervals, Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])). Walk the intervals: if the current start <= the last merged end, set last end = max(last end, current end); otherwise append. O(n log n) time. Probe: touching intervals ([1,4],[4,5]) merge; why max is needed (containment, e.g. [1,10],[2,3]); avoid a comparator with a[0] - b[0] when values can overflow.

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given an m x n grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), return the number of islands. An island is formed by connecting adjacent land cells horizontally or vertically.
solutionOutline: Scan every cell. On an unvisited '1', increment the count and flood-fill (DFS/BFS) its 4-neighbours, marking them visited (e.g. set them to '0' if mutation is allowed). O(mn) time. Probe: the recursion depth risk on a 300x300 grid of all land (use iterative BFS with ArrayDeque); Union-Find alternative; whether mutating the input is acceptable.

title: LRU Cache
statement: Design a data structure that follows the Least Recently Used cache eviction policy. Implement LRUCache(int capacity), int get(int key) which returns -1 if absent, and void put(int key, int value). When capacity is exceeded, evict the least recently used key. get and put must run in O(1) average time.
constraints:
1 <= capacity <= 3000
At most 2 * 10^5 calls to get and put.
solutionOutline: Combine a HashMap<Integer, Node> with a doubly linked list using head and tail sentinels. get: move the node to the front. put: update and move to the front, or insert at the front and evict tail.prev when size > capacity (remove it from the map too). O(1) for both. Acceptable shortcut to discuss: LinkedHashMap(capacity, 0.75f, true) with removeEldestEntry. Follow-ups: thread safety (a lock around operations, or ConcurrentHashMap plus a careful design); TTL support.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
examples:
Input: nums = [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2
Output: [1,2]

Input: nums = [1], k = 1
Output: [1]
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
k is in the range [1, number of unique elements]
solutionOutline: Count with a HashMap, then either (a) a min-heap of size k ordered by count: O(n log k), or (b) bucket sort where bucket[count] lists values, scanned from high to low: O(n). Probe: why a min-heap rather than a max-heap for top-k, tie handling, and memory for huge inputs (streaming, Count-Min Sketch as an approximate answer).

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without duplicate characters.
examples:
Input: s = "abcabcbb"
Output: 3   ("abc")

Input: s = "pwwkew"
Output: 3   ("wke")
constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4
s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
solutionOutline: Sliding window with a map from character to last index (or int[128] for ASCII). For each right: if the char was seen at index >= left, move left = lastIndex + 1. Update best = max(best, right - left + 1). O(n) time. Common bug: moving left backwards (use max). Probe: a Unicode-safe version and the space complexity O(min(n, alphabet)).
